questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Seeing that I did my mandatory exchange last year in the countryside of Korea, it was crucial for me that I had an opportunity to do another exchange in the capital city. This was both because of personal reasons (I have family there) but also because of the broader knowledge and perspective I would be able to achieve because of the experience of both the countryside and the big city. Because I study Korean Studies, this aspect was extremely important to me since it contributed to my understanding and knowledge of Korea.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found it very easy. The host university was very good at giving all the informations needed and pin out specific deadlines, etc., at their communication channel. They were really quick at responding to emails as well, so overall, I was very satisfied with it.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Before arriving, I was connected to a buddy who was a big help. She had contacted me a week before I arrived and helped me with how to check in to the dormitory. My flight was delayed so I couldn’t arrive to the dormitory during the check-in time but my buddy helped me and so did the dormitory office. So I was still able to check in even though it was in the middle of the night.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The directions to the dormitory could be a bit better.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: On campus dormitory. I had a single room with my own bathroom, balcony and fridge.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: In the dormitory building that I lived in, there was a big kitchenette on every floor. The kitchenette had two big tables with chairs, a hot/cold water dispenser, mini oven and a microwave. The kitchenette was cleaned every day by the staff.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: They should know, that it is possible to apply for a single-room.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process is always stressful since it is a first-comes-first-served system, and if you are not in Korea at the time of registration, you have to be up in the middle of the night with bad internet reception because it is a korean website. So a good advice would definitely be to have several extra courses at hand because you most likely won’t be able to register all your highest priorities. AND to check out the registration process thoroughly beforehand!

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There is no help for the first registration process. But the first week of the semester is a trial and error, so I would recommend to register for a lot of courses and then try them out during the first week. During the two first weeks some courses will suddenly have more available seats and you will be able to find out which courses you like or not, and you have the opportunity to register and leave courses during this time.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successful with my registration but I think it was because 50% of my courses were graduate courses and they are “easier” to get a seat at because there aren’t as many graduate students as undergraduate students.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Register for a lot of courses! Both graduate and undergraduate, if possible. You have one or two weeks in the beginning of the semester to drop some of the courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The undergraduate courses are very different from an undergraduate course in Denmark. The academic level is lower but the system and criteria are very different. The graduate courses are very similar to courses in Denmark, and the academic level is slightly lower but again, the system and criteria are different so it is difficult to compare. But academically, my experience was that the levels are almost the same.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was quite the same. It wasn’t completely different or incomprehensible.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Korean Ceramics (Undergraduate and aimed at exchange students)
Korean Heritage (Undergraduate and aimed at exchange student)
Gender Relations in Korea (Graduate)
Sexuality and Capitalism in Asia (Graduate and was about women’s studies and feminist theory)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Korean Ceramics (Undergraduate and aimed at exchange students)
The ceramics course was a great opportunity to meet other exchange students and learn about Korean pottery while working with clay yourself. It was a nice break from the other heavy academic courses. And the professor was really nice and kind.

Korean Heritage (Undergraduate and aimed at exchange student)
This course was a lecture-structured course and was about the cultural and religious heritage of Korea. Even though the topics could be a bit historical and kind of boring, the professor was very passionate and funny which made the courses much more interesting. Quite often, the professor brought some artifacts, food and/or drinks to share with the class so we could “experience” some of the heritage of Korea. 

Gender Relations in Korea (Graduate)
This graduate course was really amazing. The professor was extremely kind, funny and helpful. The focus of the class was on women in Korea and was discussion based, and the professor facilitated this perfectly.  We had many great and important discussions, and the academic level was on the same level as in Denmark. it was without a doubt my favorite course. 
 
These three courses were all amazing in their own way.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had expected that I was going to spend a lot of money on personal spending but it is not a necessity. One could definitely go by without spending as much money on oneself.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries in Korea are insanely expensive. Especially fruits and vegetables. So, if you want to save money, don’t cook at home. You can find really cheap and delicious local restaurants everywhere.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The host university did several social activities for the exchange students. Both cultural, athletic and social.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of opportunities to meet other students and be social, you just have to reach out and/or participate when these opportunities are there.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There is a lot to see and/or experience in Korea, and, I think, it is fairly easy to be tourist/foreigner there. I would recommend that you do a bit of research beforehand and figure what you really want to try or experience, and then figure out when and where you can do it, because when you arrive and the semester begins time will fly by quickly.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It can be very difficult to adjust to the Korean culture, so I would recommend that you find your base and maybe some friends, so you aren’t all alone.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Koreans can be difficult to get to know and befriend. Mostly because of the language barrier. And some older people can be extremely rude to foreigners…

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I can’t choose. A culture is a culture. Some aspects are lovely, some are not, but they are both a part of a whole culture.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Register for a lot of courses
Be patient, and if you have further questions don’t hesitate to contact them
Be respectful and understanding. You are a visitor and have chosen to be a visitor, so if things are different than what they are at home, you are not entitled to demand it to change for you.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Think about why you want to go on exchange, and what you hope to achieve from it. And if possible, reach out to other students who have been on exchange at the same university so you can adjust your expectations.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Everything. The whole experience in it self.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Everything. It is extremely rewarding to be on exchange but is is also extremely hard and difficult.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
